h: One demand, two cities: barricades in Delhi, a fair in Mumbai
dek: Protests on Gandhi Jayanti demanding the Chief Election Commissioner's resignation showed that the way police behave decides the shape a protest takes.
body: On 2 October, people in Delhi and Mumbai took to the streets with the same demand: Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar must resign. The anger is rooted in the clean-up of the voter rolls known as SIR. Critics allege that under its cover, the names of lakhs of genuine voters have vanished from the lists.

One thing in this Scroll ground report is striking. The questions are not only coming from outside. Within the Commission itself, two election commissioners have recorded written dissent fourteen times in ten months on decisions linked to SIR.

The report then sets the two cities side by side. In Delhi, police blocked roads, shut twelve metro stations, restricted the internet and detained around seven hundred people. Several organisers were picked up before they could even reach the protest site. The result: a small crowd.
In Mumbai, permission had not been granted, yet more than ten thousand people gathered. There were speeches and songs, and the mood was like a fair. Instead of confrontation, there was celebration.

The difference shows in the voices the reporters heard. A student in Delhi blamed the low turnout on the absence of opposition parties. A taxi driver in Mumbai finds the whole system rotten. And some young people called these small sparks that must be kept alive.
nazar: The right to vote is the foundation of democracy, and names struck off the voter rolls usually hurt those with the fewest papers: migrant workers, the poor, the homeless and marginalised communities.
The report is also a reminder that within the same country, the right to protest takes a different shape the moment you change cities.
sawal: Does even the right to vote now depend on paperwork?
ref: SIR
Special Intensive Revision of the voter rolls. Officials check house to house and the list is prepared afresh.
Chief Election Commissioner
Head of the Election Commission, which has two other election commissioners. The Commission is responsible for running the country's elections.
ank: times written dissent was recorded within the Commission itself

h: Those whose names were erased came to Shivaji Park
dek: More than 25 lakh names were cut from Bengal's voter list, and people from Murshidabad who work as labourers in Mumbai are asking what they did wrong.
body: On the evening of 2 October, Gandhi Jayanti, around ten thousand people gathered at Shivaji Park in Mumbai. The demand was one: Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar must resign. The crowd had familiar faces like Shabana Azmi, Naseeruddin Shah and Vishal Bhardwaj, but the PARI reporter's eye stayed on those who have come to this city from hundreds of kilometres away to earn a living.

In West Bengal's Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of the voter list, more than 25 lakh people were declared ineligible in the name of 'logical discrepancies'. Most of them do not even know how to get their names added back.

Mustaqim S.K., 35, from Panchgram in Murshidabad, had his name cut. So did his father and brothers, while his mother's and sisters' names survived. He has a passport, a voter card, a PAN card and educational certificates. Still, no one has told him why his name was removed.

Hasanuzzaman, from Saheb Nagar village in the same district, has been a construction worker in Mumbai for four years. He lives with other young men in Saki Naka and earns about Rs 700 a day. His name survived, and he even voted in the April Assembly election. He came anyway, because in his area people who have lived in the same place for fifteen years are having their names cut.

In the crowd was also a teenage girl holding a copy of the Constitution, who had joined the July protests too. The report says this was the second big protest on the issue across the country, and the crowd kept growing as evening fell.
nazar: A name cut from the voter list is no small clerical error; it is a blow to a citizen's most basic right. And the names cut are usually of those whose voices are already weak: migrant workers and poor families who have neither the time nor the money to keep running to government offices.
Trust in the process that democracy rests on will return only when the reason for every deleted name is given in writing, and there is an easy, free way to get it added back.
sawal: If someone has all the papers, why was their name cut?
ref: SIR (Special Intensive Revision)
The Election Commission process in which the voter list is checked afresh and voters must show documents proving they are eligible.
PARI
People's Archive of Rural India, a platform started by journalist P. Sainath that records the lives of rural and working people. It can be read free in many Indian languages.

h: If they allege rigging, why is the opposition still contesting?
dek: Amid calls to boycott elections, opposition parties say leaving the field would only make defeat more certain.
body: If the opposition believes elections are being rigged, why is it contesting them? The question grew louder after 25 September, when activist Abhijit Dipke openly called for a boycott of elections.
The case for a boycott is simple. Taking part in such an election stamps it as legitimate. And if the opposition walks out, a large movement could rise on the streets.

Opposition leaders disagree. Congress's Amitabh Dubey points to Bangladesh, where a boycott ended with the ruling party winning a majority big enough to change even the Constitution. For Trinamool's Derek O'Brien, a boycott means handing your ground over to someone else, and betraying the workers who have toiled for the party for years.

The article also lists the practical problems. If you don't contest, donations dry up, the organisation starts to fall apart, and new outfits that run at the will of those in power spring up in the empty space.
So for now the opposition's strategy is two-fold: contest elections, and keep up the fight for fair elections too.
nazar: This piece connects with the first report on this page, where the absence of opposition parties at the Delhi protest was questioned.
The real question is uncomfortable: when trust in institutions is shaking, is staying in the game a strategy or a compulsion? And where is the voter's voice in this debate?
sawal: Is staying in the fight courage or compulsion?
ref: Election boycott
When a party or group refuses, in protest, to contest or vote in an election, so that the election's legitimacy is called into question.

h: The Nandigram bypoll: one field, and almost a single player
dek: In this bypoll five months after power changed hands in Bengal, opposition posters are hard to find, but complaints against the police are everywhere.
body: Nandigram goes to a bypoll on 6 October. According to the report, the seat belonged to Chief Minister Suvendu Adhikari, and the BJP government in the state is only five months old. The BJP has fielded Hasirani Rath, mother of a slain political associate. Facing her are Milan Pradhan of the Congress and Shanti Gopal Giri of the CPI.

The Scroll reporter saw a one-sided contest on the ground. BJP flags and banners cover the roads. The Congress campaign runs on a single e-rickshaw, whose sound is drowned out by the BJP's loudspeaker vehicle. Most Trinamool workers have switched sides.

The opposition's allegations are serious: old cases reopened to detain workers, false cases against polling agents, and an attack on the CPI candidate. The BJP candidate laughs these off; according to her, you need binoculars to find the opposition.

The most interesting voices are the voters'. A Muslim voter talks of going with the ruling party as a practical calculation; an elderly Hindu woman is fed up with the previous government. Most people have accepted that the result is decided in advance.
nazar: Nandigram is the place where, in 2007, a farmers' movement against land acquisition changed Bengal's politics. For the opposition to become so weak there today is a warning for democracy, no matter who holds power.
sawal: When there is no real contest left, whose election is it?
ref: Bypoll
An election held for a single seat when it falls vacant between general elections.

h: The court that could not see harassment
dek: A former judge of Pakistan's Supreme Court asks: is workplace harassment only harassment when there is sexual desire behind it?
body: Pakistan's new Federal Constitutional Court recently overturned a ruling of the Islamabad High Court. The court said that under the 2010 workplace harassment law, only behaviour of a sexual nature would count as harassment.

Justice Shah considers this thinking wrong from the root. In his view, the law flows from the right to human dignity. In the case in question, things like making obscene sketches and crude remarks had already been proved, yet the court dismissed the case without discussing the evidence.

He lists precedents from around the world: a landmark ruling of the US Supreme Court, the courts of Canada and India, and International Labour Organization Convention 190. The gist of all of them is the same. Harassment does not need desire behind it; demeaning someone because of their gender is also harassment. Pakistan's own 2022 amendment covers such discrimination, whether sexual or not.

The article also questions how the court went about it. Earlier precedents were ignored, the Attorney General was not heard, and no amicus curiae was appointed. There was not a single woman judge on the bench. And the court itself was created by a controversial constitutional amendment that has left the country with two top courts.
Justice Shah concludes that the true test of a constitutional court is not its power but the rights it protects.
nazar: In India, the path against workplace harassment opened with the Vishaka guidelines (1997) and then the 2013 law. This debate next door is a reminder that making a law is not enough; who interprets it, and how, matters just as much.
The question applies to our offices too: how effective are complaints committees, and how many women sit at the table where decisions are made?
sawal: How many women sit in the seat of justice?
ref: Federal Constitutional Court
A new court in Pakistan created by the 27th constitutional amendment to hear constitutional cases. It is highly controversial.
Amicus curiae
An expert lawyer appointed to assist the court, who does not represent either side.

h: Russia's ageing nuclear plants: who will pay to shut them down?
dek: A climate activist warns that Russia is selling reactors around the world while putting off the reckoning for its own old reactors at home.
body: The world talks about Russia's nuclear weapons threats, but another danger is quietly growing: Russia's own ageing nuclear power plants. The state company has 35 reactors in line for closure. Shutting them down safely is estimated to cost 21 billion euros, and there is no money arranged for 18.7 billion euros of that.

Around 7.7 lakh cubic metres of radioactive waste from the Soviet era is already lying around, and these reactors will produce another 8 lakh cubic metres. The experience of other countries is alarming. In Lithuania, 3.3 billion euros had been spent on one plant by 2020 and the work was not even half done. In Germany, the cost for one plant rose from one billion to ten billion euros.

According to the writer, Russia is putting off the costly stages in the name of long-term storage. The cost of the war has eaten up the environment budget, and independent watchdogs have been suppressed. He recalls that the Soviet government hid the 1957 Mayak disaster for 32 years.
He suggests that countries where Russia is building nuclear projects should keep their own emergency plans ready and raise these questions on international platforms.
nazar: This question is not far from us. Tamil Nadu's Kudankulam plant was built with Russian help, and so was neighbouring Bangladesh's Rooppur plant. In debates on nuclear power, the cost of shutting plants down and the bill for the waste are often left out.
sawal: The power is for today; who will pay for the waste tomorrow?
ref: Decommissioning
Safely shutting down a nuclear plant at the end of its life, dismantling the structure and disposing of the radioactive waste. It takes decades.
ank: euros, cost of shutting down 35 reactors

h: Taking over the textbooks: an attempt to take away Palestinian children's history
dek: In East Jerusalem, the number of Palestinian students studying from Israeli-approved textbooks has doubled in a year.
body: In occupied East Jerusalem, 45,000 Palestinian students now study an Israeli-approved curriculum, double the number last year. Jabareen writes that international humanitarian law does not allow an occupying power to change the education system or impose a new curriculum.
Israel argues that Palestinian textbooks teach hatred. The writer points out that several studies, including one funded by the US State Department, do not support this claim.

So what is being removed from the books? According to research: references to the flag, the national anthem, sovereignty and the reality of occupation. One study found that in some places Palestine was replaced with Israel. Ideas like the Nakba and the refugees' right of return are also targets.
Jabareen concludes that this is a fight not about hatred but about national consciousness. Whoever controls the institutions is deciding in what shape children learn their own history.
nazar: The debate over removing or changing chapters of history in the syllabus comes up again and again in India too. A generation's memory becomes whatever survives in its textbooks.
sawal: When history is removed from the textbook, is it erased from memory too?
ref: Nakba
An Arabic word meaning catastrophe. It is how the loss of homes and displacement of lakhs of Palestinians during Israel's creation in 1948 is remembered.

h: The debt trap and the price of freedom
dek: Senegalese economist Yassine Fall says the IMF's new package is the same old medicine that has been making the disease worse for forty years.
body: In July 2024, Senegal found out that debt equal to nearly a quarter of the country's GDP had been hidden in the government's books. Debt that had been reported as 74 percent at the end of 2023 turned out to actually be 99 percent. Total government debt is now above 130 percent of GDP.
It was in this anger that people voted the Pastef party to power in November 2024, on a promise of change and sovereignty. Now the IMF has announced a 2.2 billion dollar loan programme.

Fall argues that IMF programmes in Africa have brought only stagnation and poverty. Prescriptions of privatisation, cuts in government spending and a free hand for markets deepened the debt crises of countries like Zambia and Ethiopia.

She suggests that the people themselves audit the debt and see which loans were legitimate. The tax burden should fall not on ordinary people but on mining and oil companies and the rich. Every new loan should need Parliament's approval, and the accounts of oil and gas earnings should be open.

On a larger scale, she talks of a joint front of indebted African countries, a 20 to 30 year breather on debt repayment, and freedom from the CFA franc, an old colonial currency. For her, the real question is whether Senegal wants a better version of the old policy or to be rid of it.
nazar: India itself went to the IMF's door in 1991, and neighbouring Sri Lanka took the same road after going bankrupt in 2022. This debate over debt and conditions is not foreign to us.
Solidarity among Global South countries comes up again and again in India's foreign policy too. Senegal's debate is its real test.
sawal: Freedom from debt, or a new chain of conditions?
ref: IMF
International Monetary Fund, which lends to countries in crisis, often with strict economic conditions.
CFA franc
A shared currency of several West and Central African countries, with roots in the French colonial era.

h: The Himalaya's warning: change, or be wiped out
dek: After Nepal's terrible flood, Sunita Narain asks when we will learn from the disasters that keep striking the mountains.
body: More than 1,300 people died in the flood that hit Nepal on 26 August. Near the Langtang Lirung peak, a mass of ice and rock of about 14.2 crore cubic metres broke off. It formed natural dams in the rivers, and when they burst, the settlements below were washed away.
Narain does not see this as a one-off. Chamoli in 2021, Sikkim in 2024, Himachal in 2025: each time the story is similar.
She gives two reasons. First, rising heat, which is making glaciers unstable and slopes weaker. Second, thoughtless development: hydropower dams and tunnels with no plan to protect the slopes.

She says the world has already crossed the 1.5 degree limit, and beyond it every disaster will be bigger than the last. Small fixes will not do; the belief that nature can be controlled has to change.
nazar: The roads, tunnels and dams being built in Uttarakhand, Himachal and Sikkim are our own debate. In the mountains, the first blow falls on villages that were never even asked.
sawal: Development in the mountains for whom, and who pays the price?
ref: The 1.5 degree limit
The Paris climate agreement goal that the Earth's temperature should not rise more than 1.5 degrees Celsius above pre-industrial levels.

h: A father from Bihar, swept away in Nepal's flood
dek: The Bhotekoshi flood uprooted Bihari workers settled in Betrawati, and the families who returned home have received no compensation.
body: On 26 August, a glacier broke in Nepal's Himalaya, and along with a landslide it sent such a flood down the Bhotekoshi river that Betrawati, near the Tibet border, was almost wiped out. According to the PARI report, around 1,300 bodies were found and more than five thousand people are still missing.

About 30 Bihari workers worked in Betrawati; only around 15 survived. Nandlal Sahni, 51, from East Champaran, ran a scrap business there. That morning the family was having breakfast when a warning call came. Everyone ran towards higher ground. Nandlal kept pushing his sons towards safety and was himself swept away by the water. Later a survivor told his son that even as he was being carried away, Nandlal had held him up.

Deeplal, 20, had left school after Class 8 to help his father; now he is the head of the household. His uncle Harilal crossed the border within 24 hours and brought the younger brothers back from a relief camp. The business stock, a tractor, motorcycles, documents: everything was washed away. The body was never found, so the last rites were done in Tharghatwa village with an effigy made of grass, and even that cost became a burden on the family.

The Sahni community has fished for generations, but shrinking rivers took away that livelihood and people began heading north, to Nepal. On this side of the 1,751-kilometre open border, people like Harilal feel Kathmandu is closer than Patna.

The Bihar government has announced no ex gratia payment for these families. In such tragedies, Rs 4 lakh is usually given from the Chief Minister's Relief Fund, but this time there has been no announcement.
nazar: This story shows the double blow of the climate crisis, which falls on the poorest: first the river shrank and the livelihood went, then the mountain broke and lives were lost. And a migrant working between two countries becomes no government's responsibility.
Many families cross the open border back and forth for work, but in a disaster there is no shared system to count them or help them. This gap has to be filled.
sawal: When a worker dies earning across the border, whose account does it go into?
ref: Glacier collapse
When a glacier or a lake formed by it suddenly bursts, the rivers below flood heavily. Such disasters are rising in the Himalaya as the Earth warms.
India-Nepal open border
Under a 1950 treaty, citizens of both countries can travel and work in each other's country without a passport or visa.

h: Refugee budgets shrink, the displaced struggle more
dek: Heavy cuts in the UN refugee agency's funding are shutting down clinics, maternity wards and child protection programmes.
body: By the end of 2025, the number of people forced from their homes worldwide had reached about 11.8 crore. In exactly the same period, the budget of UNHCR, the agency that helps them, kept shrinking.

According to Dawn's editorial, the agency had 5.2 billion dollars in 2024, down to 3.9 billion in 2025, while it needs about 8.5 billion dollars a year. By the end of July 2026, only 32 percent of the money needed had come in. The agency has had to cut more than a quarter of its staff, nearly five thousand people.

The impact is visible on the ground. In Chad, clinics and maternity wards for refugees have closed. In parts of Ethiopia, child protection programmes have shrunk by up to 85 percent. In Sudan, help for women and children who have suffered sexual violence hangs by a thread.
For Pakistan this is a direct issue, as it hosts more than seven lakh registered Afghan refugees.
The paper argues that today's savings are laying the foundation for a bigger crisis tomorrow. Rich donor countries should give more, and the burden should be shared fairly.
nazar: India has been home to Tibetan, Sri Lankan Tamil, Afghan and Rohingya refugees, though India has not signed the 1951 Refugee Convention.
When international aid falls, the burden finally lands on neighbouring countries and the most vulnerable people.
sawal: How big a crisis tomorrow will today's savings cause?
ref: UNHCR
The UN refugee agency, which protects and helps people uprooted by war, persecution or disaster.

chart.title: UNHCR's annual budget
chart.note: By July 2026, only 32 percent of the money needed had come in

h: A failed execution and double standards
dek: In the US, an attempt to execute a woman by lethal injection failed. The writer asks: if this had happened in Iran, what would the world have said?
body: On 3 October, Christa Pike, 50, was to be executed in Tennessee, USA. She would have been the first woman to be executed in the state since 1820. The lethal injection procedure failed, and she was taken to hospital alive.

Pike was convicted at the age of 18 of murdering a fellow student. She suffered sexual abuse from childhood and struggled with mental illness. Afraid of the pain of the injection, she had asked to die by firing squad, which was refused.
Fernández's pointed question: if Iran had made such a blunder while executing a similarly broken woman, the US would have led the condemnation. Here there was no such outcry.

She also lays out the numbers. Since 1973, more than 200 people sentenced to death have later been proved innocent. Black people are 12 percent of the US population but 40 percent of death row prisoners. For her, this punishment is less about justice and more a weapon of the powerful.
nazar: The death penalty remains in India too. In 2015, the Law Commission recommended abolishing it except in terrorism cases. Here too, questions keep being raised about why so many of those sentenced are poor and marginalised.
sawal: Why anger at another country's executions, and silence about our own?
ref: Law Commission
A body that advises the Government of India on reforming laws. Its 262nd report, in 2015, was on the death penalty.

h: Pakistan's hopes of friendship with Russia, and India's long shadow
dek: Ahead of the SCO meeting in Islamabad, a Pakistani security expert asks whether Moscow will really come closer.
body: Pakistan has big hopes from the Shanghai Cooperation Organisation meeting to be held in Islamabad. If President Putin comes, Pakistan will see it as a major turn in the region's politics. The focus is on defence cooperation, and also on a rail corridor to Moscow through Central Asia and Iran.

Rana brings these hopes down to earth with numbers. Trade between Pakistan and Russia is less than 50 crore dollars, while India-Russia trade is about 69 billion dollars. In defence the gap is even wider. Russia's military ties with India are decades old and deep; with Pakistan they are selective.

According to him, Russia sees Pakistan not as a strategic partner but as a way to keep its presence in the region. Their interests in Afghanistan differ, Russia will not want to spoil its ties with India, and Pakistan also leans towards the US.
The article ends on an interesting question: if India and Pakistan decided to live in peace, the region's entire calculation would change.
nazar: It is rare to see India viewed this way from next door. Rana's last point is for both countries: peace between them is better than becoming pawns in the game of big powers.
sawal: If Delhi and Islamabad choose peace, who loses?
ref: SCO
Shanghai Cooperation Organisation, whose members include China, Russia, India, Pakistan, Iran and several Central Asian countries.

h: Botswana at sixty: the sparkle of diamonds and the question of what comes after
dek: A country that challenges the story of African failure, which took its mining wealth to its people, but now has to find a path beyond diamonds.
body: At independence in 1966, Botswana was among the poorest countries in the world. Sixty years later it is an upper-middle-income country. Between 1965 and 1980 its economy grew on average 13.9 percent a year, and today its per capita income is higher than even South Africa's.

According to Mhaka, the secret lies not in the diamonds but in how they were managed. The government kept a half share in diamond mining and put part of the earnings into a fund for the future. This saved it from the fate in which mining wealth gets stuck in a few hands.

The results show in society too. Poverty fell from 30.6 percent in 2002-03 to 14.5 percent in 2022. Ninety-eight percent of pregnant women living with HIV get treatment, and the country has set an example in preventing transmission from mother to child.

But the danger is also clear. Diamonds make up about 90 percent of goods exports. With lab-grown diamonds and falling demand, the economy shrank in 2024 and 2025. Unemployment is 21 percent, and nearly 29 percent among the young. Now the country has to build an economy beyond diamonds.
nazar: Despite the mineral wealth of Jharkhand, Odisha and Chhattisgarh, the poverty of their Adivasi (indigenous) areas puts the same question before us: the wealth comes out from under the ground, but who does it reach?
sawal: Who has the first claim on the wealth of the mines?
ref: Resource curse
When a country rich in oil, diamonds or minerals sees poverty, corruption and instability grow despite that abundance.

h: Three years after 7 October: who is telling the story now?
dek: A Pakistani journalist writes that the destruction of Gaza changed how the world sees things, and Palestinians learned to tell their own story.
body: In the Hamas attack of 7 October 2023, about 1,200 people were killed in Israel and more than 250 were taken hostage. At the time, the world's sympathy was with Israel.

According to Muna Khan, three years of the Gaza war have turned this picture around. Israel's argument of seeing every action through the lens of victimhood has lost its force. People no longer accept that condemning Hamas requires staying silent about Palestinian pain.

A big reason for the change is that Palestinian journalists and ordinary people are recording their own devastation. Foreign journalists were kept out, and 191 Palestinian journalists have been killed in Israeli attacks.

In a 2026 Pew survey, 67 percent of people across 36 countries held a negative view of Israel, including 60 percent in the US. The writer accepts that this will not rebuild homes, but Israel's confidence that the world will blindly accept its story has been broken.
nazar: When the doors of big media are shut, the people themselves become witnesses. This lesson is not Gaza's alone.
sawal: When journalists themselves are targets, who will bring us the truth?
ref: Pew Research Center
A non-partisan US research organisation that conducts public opinion surveys around the world.

h: The wealth beneath our feet that no one accounts for
dek: Sunita Narain writes that India spends a large share of its budget on fertiliser, yet the health of its soil keeps getting worse.
body: Soil is not just dirt; it is a living world. Narain compares it to the human gut, whose health depends on countless microbes. In soil, bacteria, fungi and other micro-organisms do the same job.
But our farm policy sees soil only in terms of chemicals: nitrogen, phosphorus and potash. The government spends Rs 1.71 lakh crore on fertiliser subsidy, about 3 percent of the budget.

The result is the opposite of what was intended. An analysis of 1.3 crore soil health cards issued between 2023 and 2025 showed that chemical fertiliser use rose 20 percent, yet soil quality fell. Half the samples were low in organic carbon.
Narain calls for ways to measure the biological health of soil and for more diversity in crops. Healthy soil also absorbs carbon from the air, which makes it a weapon in the climate fight too.
nazar: The health of the soil is directly tied to the farmer's pocket and to our plates. The burden of rising fertiliser use and falling yields is finally borne by small farmers.
sawal: Are we feeding the soil fertiliser, or life?
ref: Soil health card
A government scheme in which a farmer's soil is tested and the farmer is told which nutrients it lacks.

h: In Sudan, America's pressure gamble has backfired
dek: An expert argues that sanctioning only one side does not stop a war, and that the US has ended up isolating itself.
body: Sudan's war is now more than three years old. During the UN General Assembly, the US made a big pressure play: army chief General al-Burhan would be allowed to speak there only if he signed an unconditional ceasefire.

According to Hudson, this rested on a misunderstanding. The warring sides are fighting not in hope of victory but for their survival, and in such a situation diplomatic pressure alone does not change the outcome of a war.

The second mistake is one-sidedness. Sanctions were placed only on the army, while the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces were treated as more cooperative, though the writer does not trust their talk of peace. Calling both sides illegitimate also upset partners like Saudi Arabia.

The writer recalls that twenty years of US sanctions had failed to bend Sudan's rulers before as well. If peace is the aim, the US has to talk to both warring sides, not apply pressure meant to change the regime.
nazar: Sudan's war is among the world's largest humanitarian crises, yet it is almost missing from our news. In the diplomacy of big powers, the lives of ordinary people are often the cheapest.
sawal: Can peace be bought by punishing one side?
ref: Rapid Support Forces (RSF)
Sudan's paramilitary force, which has been at war with the army since April 2023.

h: From stability to growth? A warning from the paper next door
dek: As Pakistan's prime minister makes his announcement, a Dawn editorial says growth that leans on consumption and construction will lead back into the same crisis.
body: Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif has announced that Pakistan will now move beyond managing crises towards growth driven by jobs and exports. He points to rising foreign exchange reserves, money sent home from abroad, IT exports and returning investment.
Dawn asks whether this is real change or just an announcement. The paper argues that industries raised behind tariff walls and on subsidies never became able to compete.

Pakistan keeps returning to crisis because growth built on consumption and construction does not earn as much foreign exchange as it needs. According to the editorial, economic stability is not a barrier to growth but its first condition.

The road runs through deep reforms: governance, competition, productivity, energy, and investment in people's education and health. Export factories, modern farming and small industries are the only foundation for lasting growth.
nazar: The complaint of growth without jobs is common in India too. This debate next door is a reminder that shiny numbers and a job for a young person are two different things.
sawal: If the numbers rise but jobs don't come, whose growth is it?
ref: Foreign exchange reserves
Foreign currencies such as dollars held by the central bank, used to pay for imports and foreign debt.

h: When question marks start to disappear
dek: Tribhuvan's satire says democracy dies not when language dies, but when grammar shrinks.
body: Tribhuvan tells the story of democracy through punctuation marks. For him, the question mark is not mere grammar; it is the freedom to ask questions. And dictatorship loves the full stop, after which there is no debate.

The sharpest point of the satire is that the question is not censored; the structure of the sentence is simply changed. Instead of 'what happened?', it is written 'this happened', and the question quietly disappears.

Then each mark is given a democratic job. The comma is a place to breathe and to disagree, brackets a corner for private thought, the three dots an admission of incompleteness, and the footnote the place where uncomfortable truths survive. Sanskrit's danda, Urdu's reversed question mark and Persian quotation marks are also part of this family.
In the end, the writer warns that when questions go missing, people begin to accept silence as normal, and oppression becomes an invisible habit.
nazar: Hindi satire has an old tradition of catching power through language. This piece is a new and witty link in that tradition.
sawal: When did you last put a question mark on a government statement?
ref: Punctuation marks
Marks that show a pause, a question or a feeling in a sentence, such as the full stop (।), the comma (,) and the question mark (?).

h: Ghalib, whom every generation reads anew
dek: The introduction to Pankaj Parashar's book Ghalib ke Sau Rang (A Hundred Shades of Ghalib), which explains why Ghalib does not fit into any single box.
body: Great literature is what every generation reads again in its own way. That is how Parashar arrives at Ghalib. This nineteenth-century poet writes about questions like love, death, identity and the meaning of life, which never grow old.

The writer suggests reading Ghalib in several layers: the layer of the Persian and Urdu language; the layer of philosophy, which raises questions but does not force answers; the historical layer of his changing times; and the psychological layer of the inner human being.
He stresses that calling Ghalib only a Sufi, only a romantic or only a philosopher makes him smaller. His greatness lies in weaving all of these together in extremely tight language.
The introduction concludes that reading Ghalib is not a task you finish but an ongoing practice, one that changes the reader more than the poet.
nazar: In the shared heritage of Hindi and Urdu, Ghalib is the strongest bridge. In a time of hatred, reading him is also a kind of answer.
sawal: Is reading Ghalib a way of reading yourself?
ref: Mirza Ghalib
(1797-1869) A great poet of Urdu and Persian who saw the end of the Mughal era and 1857.

h: Before you compose the tune, read the director's mind
dek: Anirudh Sharma's piece on the film journey of composer duo Dilip-Sameer Sen, and its limits.
body: In the world of Hindi film music, a good tune alone is not enough. Through the experiences of Dilip Sen and Sameer Sen, Anirudh Sharma shows that to last here, you have to understand what the director likes.

One story involves Yash Chopra. When their first tunes were rejected, Dilip Sen listened closely to the music of Chopra's earlier films and recognised the colour of Pahadi in it. A new tune made in that colour was approved, and it became the song Dil Ne Dil Se Kya Kaha (What did the heart say to the heart).
Something similar happened with another director, who pointed to an old song. The composer understood its structure and created a tune in the same mood, which was liked at once.
The bitter truth of the piece is that despite these successes, the duo stayed mostly confined to small-budget films. The gap between talent and opportunity is an old story of the film world.
nazar: The stories of the film world's unsung craftspeople are an important part of our cultural history, often buried under the glitter of the stars.
sawal: Which matters more, talent or opportunity?
ref: Pahadi
A raga of Hindustani music rooted in the folk tunes of the hills. Many famous Hindi film songs are based on it.

h: Gandhi, locked inside school essays
dek: Gagan Talreja's wry piece on how Gandhi was learnt by rote for exam answer sheets, but never made it into our lives.
body: There has hardly ever been a Hindi exam without an essay on Gandhi. Gagan Talreja examines this habit. According to him, teachers felt that leaving out the Father of the Nation might invite displeasure, and Gandhi's principles were as easy to memorise as they were hard to practise.
Truth, non-violence, sacrifice and the freedom struggle: these four pegs became the frame of every essay. Essays on Nehru or Subhas came up once in a while; Gandhi came almost every time.

The writer shows how children kept repeating the same worn-out sentences without understanding them. He also creates a funny sample essay in which principles and made-up anecdotes are cooked into a hotchpotch, and that is perhaps the truth of our education.

He concludes that Gandhi remained a prisoner of words in school notebooks. The hope is that some generation of rote learners will one day take him out of the books and give him a place in their lives.
nazar: Every Gandhi Jayanti brings a flood of ritual tributes. This piece asks: do we really know the idea we only remember?
sawal: Remembering Gandhi is easy; why is living him so hard?
ref: Bela
Hindwi's prose section, which publishes essays, memoirs, diaries and commentary.

h: The Gandhi that Pakistan never wanted to understand
dek: An excerpt from Vivek Shukla's new book 1947: Vibhajan ke Shesh Sawal (1947: The Remaining Questions of Partition), which remembers the Gandhi who wanted to go to Lahore after Partition.
body: The excerpt begins with an irony. Gandhi was killed because his killer believed he stood with Muslims and Pakistan, and yet in many of that same Pakistan's textbooks he has been turned into a Hindu leader who stood against Muslims.

Shukla recalls that had he not been killed in January 1948, Gandhi was to go to Pakistan in early February, without police or army, relying only on the people there. The aim was to bring back some goodwill on both sides after the fires of Partition.

A moving part of the book is about the dargah (Sufi shrine) of Bakhtiyar Kaki in Mehrauli. Rioters had damaged it, Gandhi fasted, and three days before he was killed he went there and assured Muslims that they did not need to go to Pakistan. The writer regrets that today there is no record of this visit at the dargah at all.

The excerpt also says that in Pakistan's liberal intellectual circles, the way Gandhi is seen is changing, and that facts such as Gandhi's ties to institutions like Jamia Millia Islamia are often missing from official narratives.
nazar: Published around Gandhi Jayanti, this excerpt is a reminder that Gandhi's last fight was against communal violence, and that politics on both sides has trimmed his memory to suit itself.
sawal: Both sides read only half of Gandhi; who will read him whole?
ref: Janaki Pul
A well-known Hindi literary web magazine that publishes stories, poems, translations, reviews and book excerpts.

h: The flow of the arts in Kunwar Narain's poetry
dek: Prayag Shukla's essay showing how theatre, music, painting and cinema quietly flowed through Kunwar Narain's poetry.
body: Prayag Shukla begins with a question: is the presence of other arts directly visible in a poet's work? His answer is no. It has to be searched for, and that is the task and the joy of a thoughtful reader.

In Kunwar Narain's case, this search finds an easy direction, because his interviews and life stories themselves show the way. Names like Ebrahim Alkazi, Satyajit Ray, Pandit Jasraj, Sanjukta Panigrahi and B.V. Karanth come and go naturally in his world, and he wrote an entire book on cinema.

The writer recalls that writers of that generation made a relationship with the arts a natural part of literature. Magazines like Prateek had regular film and art columns, and Kunwar Narain and Shrilal Shukla built serious discussion of film and theatre in Chhayanat.
The essay concludes that it is the influence of this tradition that today's young poets, too, have begun to see their relationship with music, dance and folk arts as part of their identity.
nazar: At a time when the arts are being split into separate boxes, this essay is a reminder of how much poetry, cinema and music have enriched one another.
sawal: To understand one art, must we pass through another?
ref: Kunwar Narain
(1927-2017) A leading Hindi poet, known for works such as Atmajayee (Self-conqueror) and Vajashrava ke Bahane (On the pretext of Vajashrava). Awarded the Jnanpith in 2005.
